answer.submission_route: The notice does not identify the managed-care organization or provide an appeal mailing address, fax number, portal, or telephone number. Therefore, the correct submission route cannot be determined from the notice. Kansas KanCare's official appeals information says that a member appeal is submitted to the member's managed-care organization (MCO), but the MCO must first be identified. Do not send the appeal to an unspecified payer. Contact the number or address on the member's insurance card or ask the provider that submitted prior authorization request POC-7321626800-52420 for the payer's appeal instructions. The KanCare appeals page is https://www.kancare.ks.gov/members/help-resources/appeals-fair-hearings/appeals.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: Ask the payer and the requesting provider, in writing, for the exact medical-necessity policy and clinical-review criteria applied to CPT 23472, including the policy title and number, effective date, criteria version, any InterQual or other proprietary criteria used, and the specific documentation considered insufficient. Include member ID W763701748 and reference number POC-7321626800-52420. Also request the complete adverse-benefit-determination record and the appeal submission instructions. The notice should be corrected or supplemented to identify the payer and provide the appeal route.

answer.notes: Kansas Medicaid/KanCare has multiple MCOs, including Healthy Blue, Sunflower, and UnitedHealthcare, and their medical policies and appeal routes differ. I retrieved a public UnitedHealthcare Community Plan policy titled "Surgery of the Shoulder," policy number CS109.Y, effective November 1, 2025, at https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/policies/medicaid-comm-plan/surgery-shoulder-cs.pdf. It lists CPT 23472, but it states that Kansas uses a separate Kansas-specific policy and directs reviewers to proprietary InterQual criteria. Nothing in the supplied notice establishes that UnitedHealthcare issued this denial, so that document cannot responsibly be identified as the governing policy. The official KanCare search result states that member appeals generally must be submitted to the MCO within 63 calendar days, which conflicts with the notice's stated 180-day deadline; the notice's specific deadline should be preserved in the appeal, while the payer should be asked to confirm the applicable deadline.

transcript.content: You are helping a patient respond to a health insurance denial. Answer precisely and only from evidence you actually retrieve. If you cannot find the governing policy, say so plainly rather than naming a document you are unsure of.

NOTICE OF ADVERSE BENEFIT DETERMINATION

Date of notice: 2026-08-02
Member: Quinn Novak
Member ID: W763701748
Plan: Medicaid (Medicaid), state of Kansas

Dear Quinn,

We reviewed the prior authorization request submitted by your provider for the following service:

    Requested service: Total shoulder replacement
    Procedure code (CPT): 23472

After review, this request is DENIED. Reason for determination: the clinical records submitted do not document an adequate trial of conservative treatment prior to the requested surgery.

This determination was made under the plan's applicable medical policy and clinical review criteria. You have the right to appeal this decision. Your appeal must be received within 180 days of the date of this notice (by 2027-01-29).

Reference number: POC-7321626800-52420


---

Above is a denial letter. Using web search as needed:

1. Identify the payer's governing medical policy for the denied procedure --
   the specific document containing the medical-necessity criteria this payer
   applies to this CPT code.
2. Give its title, policy number, URL, and effective or last-revised date.
3. Quote the medical-necessity criteria the patient must address.
4. State the appeal deadline.
5. State where and how to submit the appeal.

If no such document is publicly available, say so explicitly and explain how
the patient can obtain the criteria that were applied to them.

Another significant concern is that many of these studies are industry-sponsored or authored by device developers, which introduces potential bias into the findings. Further high-quality studies are needed to address these limitations. The InSpace™ Subacromial Tissue Spacer System (Stryker) is a minimally invasive, biodegradable balloon spacer for treating massive, inoperable rotator cuff tears (MIRCTs). According to the manufacturer, it preserves musculoskeletal and bone tissues, does not require the use of an anchor, and does not require a permanent implant. It is used as a spacer to eliminate friction between the acromion and the humeral head or rotator cuff to restore shoulder function and reduce pain. It is designed to biodegrade over the course of twelve months. In 2025a, Hayes developed an Evolving Evidence Review focused on using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer (Stryker) alone or with debridement for rotator cuff tears. After a review of full-text clinical studies and systematic reviews, it was found that there is minimal support for using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer alone or with debridement for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears. Furthermore, a review of practice guidelines and position statements determined that there is no/unclear support for using the technology alone or with debridement for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears regardless of whether spacers were used alone, with debridement, or as an adjunct to partial rotator cuff repair. In a 2025b, Evolving Evidence Review by Hayes, the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer (Stryker) was evaluated as an adjunct to partial repair of rotator cuff tears. After reviewing full-text clinical studies, and systematic reviews, it was found that there is minimal support for using the InSpace biodegradable subacromial spacer as an adjunct to partial repair for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears. Additionally, after reviewing full-text clinical practice guidelines and position statements, it was determined that there is no/unclear support for using biodegradable subacromial spacers for treating massive irreparable rotator cuff tears, regardless of whether spacers were utilized as an alternative or an adjunct to partial rotator cuff repair. For the SAB arm, 14 of 449 studies were considered eligible for inclusion, while 14 of 272 were considered eligible for inclusion in the debridement arm. In total 528 individuals eligible for inclusion in the SAB arm, 479 in the debridement arm, and 69.9% of those individuals undergoing SAB placement also underwent concomitant debridement. The findings include decreases in the visual analog scale (VAS) pain score and increases in the Constant score were found to be significantly more following debridement [–0.7 points (p < .001) and ±5.5 points (p < .001), respectively], although the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) for the VAS was not attained after either procedure. Both SAB placement and debridement significantly improved the range of motion (ROM) in forward flexion/forward elevation, internal and external rotation, and abduction (p < .001). Rates of general complication were greater following debridement versus SAB placement (5.2% ±5.6% vs. 3.5% ±6.3%, respectively; p < .001); however, there were no significant variances among SAB placement and debridement in rates of persistent symptoms necessitating a reintervention (3.3% ±6.2% vs. 3.8% ±7.3%, respectively; p = .252) or reoperation rates (5.1% ±7.6% vs. 4.8% ±8.4%, respectively; p = .552). The mean time to conversion to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (RTSA) was 11.0 versus 25.4 months, respectively, for the SAB versus debridement arm. The limitations of the analysis include inconsistencies between follow-up times, with the follow-up time associated with debridement being nearly twice as long as the follow-up time related to SAB placement, are likely attributable to the recentness of SAB use globally, which may confuse evaluations with older debridement literature given the evolution in arthroscopic surgery over time. The time to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty was not uniformly reported between studies and was decided based on either individual patient data or weighted means. Also, there was heterogeneity in using and reporting rotator cuff tears size and type, further obscuring direct comparisons. The authors concluded that while SAB placement was associated with adequate postoperative outcomes for treating MIRCTs, there was no clear advantage over debridement only. Shorter operative times combined with better postoperative results and prolonged times to conversion to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty supported debridement as a more desirable choice.
